title: Why the Tiger Balm Brothers Left Rangoon for Singapore in 1926
dek: In 1926 Aw Boon Haw and Aw Boon Par moved their late father's medicine business from Rangoon to a new factory on Singapore's Neil Road.

story.founder: Aw Boon Haw and Aw Boon Par
story.company: Eng Aun Tong (later Haw Par Corporation)
story.event: Moving the family's Tiger Balm business and headquarters from Rangoon to Singapore
story.summary: Aw Boon Haw and Aw Boon Par inherited their father Aw Chu Kin's Rangoon medicine shop, Eng Aun Tong, in 1908 and built its ointment into the Tiger Balm brand. In 1926 they moved the headquarters to Singapore and opened a factory at Neil Road; sources variously attribute the move to plans for expansion into China, humiliation after unproven police charges in Rangoon, and, in the company's telling, a tiger in the watermark of Singapore's currency. The Neil Road factory made Tiger Balm for some fifty years.
paragraphs: In 1870 Aw Chu Kin, a Hakka herbalist from Fujian, opened a small medicine shop in Rangoon and called it Eng Aun Tong, the Hall of Everlasting Peace. When he died in 1908, the business passed to his younger son, Aw Boon Par, who had been educated in English in Burma. Finding it too much to manage alone, Boon Par called his elder brother, Aw Boon Haw, back from China, where he had been sent as a boy, to run it with him.

The brothers made a brand of a family ointment. Where the formula came from is disputed: the company credits their father's revival of an old imperial recipe, while a 1992 biography by Sam King, written with the family's cooperation, credits a Burmese pharmacist, U Thaw, who gave it to Boon Par. The selling is better documented. Boon Haw visited suppliers in Thailand, Hong Kong, China and Japan, studied how goods were advertised and packaged there, and came home with a poster of a leaping tiger. The company dates the name Tiger Balm to 1909; other accounts say 1918. By the 1920s the brothers were among the richest men in Rangoon.

In 1926 they moved the headquarters to Singapore and opened a three-storey factory at the corner of Neil and Craig Roads. Why is told three ways. The Dictionary of Hong Kong Biography says they had an eye on expanding into China. A Malaysian newspaper feature says Rangoon police had charged them with opium trafficking and circulating forged banknotes; the case was never established, but the humiliation decided the move. The company's own history says Boon Haw spotted a snarling tiger in the watermark of Singapore's currency, and that settled it.

In what the company calls the busiest port in the region, the new factory produced, by its account, ten times as much as Rangoon's. Boon Haw toured small Malayan towns in a car built with a tiger's head and a horn that roared, handing out samples. When a rival oil fought them in the press, the brothers launched their own newspaper, Sin Chew Jit Poh, in 1929, partly to be sure of advertising space. The Neil Road building made Tiger Balm for some fifty years and still stands, conserved.

quote.text: If there is not sufficient depth, water will not float large ships. Upset a cupful into a small hole, and a mustard-seed will be your boat. Try to float the cup, and it will stick, from the disproportion between water and vessel.
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Whatever the brothers' real reason, the move was from one harbour to a deeper one. Zhuangzi's image puts the question as one of proportion: a vessel that sticks is not always a poor vessel, and the same ointment, made by the same family, could need different water to carry it.

reflection: Nobody now can say for certain why the Aw brothers left Rangoon: ambition, humiliation, an omen in a banknote, or some mix of the three. What the record does show is what happened once they moved. The same ointment, sold by the same two men, found a market its old home could not give it.

Zhuangzi's point is about proportion. A boat that will not float is not always a bad boat; sometimes the water is too shallow. If something you are carrying has stalled despite real effort, it is worth asking whether the trouble lies in the vessel or in the depth of water around it, before you decide to push harder.
invitation: Pick one piece of work that has stalled despite real effort. Write one sentence on what about its setting, rather than its quality, might be holding it back.

research_notes: Reasons for the 1926 move differ and the story gives all three with their sources: the Dictionary of Hong Kong Biography (Stephanie Chung Po-yin, HKU Press 2012) says the brothers moved 'with an eye on expansion into China'; the New Straits Times feature says unproven Rangoon police charges of opium trafficking and counterfeiting humiliated them into leaving (it does not say which of its references this comes from); the company's heritage page tells of a tiger in the Singapore currency watermark. A Gwulo community page mentions 'disputes with British colonial authorities' but is not cited. Tiger Balm name: 1909 (company) versus 1918 (NST). Formula: the DHKB says conflicting stories exist; NST favours Sam King's 1992 family-assisted biography (the pharmacist U Thaw); the company credits the father's revival of an imperial recipe. Names and dates: the father is Aw Chu Kin in the company and NST accounts and Aw Chi Kim in the DHKB; Boon Par's birth year is 1884 (DHKB) or 1888 (company), and the NST gives Boon Haw's birth as 1872 while the DHKB and company give 1882 (NST's own age at death implies 1882), so the story gives no birth years. Whether Boon Haw was in China in 1908: NST and the company say Boon Par called him back from China; the DHKB says his schooling ended in his mid-teens when he returned to Rangoon and does not place him in China in 1908; the story follows the two sources that agree. The National Heritage Board's Roots page says Eng Aun Tong was the name of the brothers' uncle, while the DHKB, NST and company translate it as the shop's name, Hall of Everlasting Peace; the story uses the latter. The ten-fold production figure is the company's own claim and is attributed. Following the brief for this entry, the story keeps to the business move and leaves out Aw Boon Haw's later wealth, philanthropy and wartime politics. The Singapore National Library's Infopedia pages returned a 202 holding response to the checker and are not cited.
